title: Unity is Strength: The Pawn Barrier
summary: Use the tempo gained by an obstructed enemy king to promote; compare the race with an unnecessary king move.

nodes.question: Can the lone a-pawn outrun a king that looks close enough?
nodes.explanation: Begin after ...bxc6. White has Kg2/a4 against Ke5/c6/d6/f6/h7. Black has four pawns, but c6 and d6 obstruct the king’s direct path toward a8.

branches.title: Race around the obstructing pawns
commentary: Begin after ...bxc6. White has Kg2/a4 against Ke5/c6/d6/f6/h7. Black has four pawns, but c6 and d6 obstruct the king’s direct path toward a8.
a5 uses the winning tempo immediately. The white king does not need to join the race; Black must navigate around its own c6 and d6 pawns.
Kd5 approaches from below the pawn barrier. The occupied d6 square prevents the more direct king approach through that square.
a6 keeps running. Moving the white king instead would give the defender time to catch the pawn.
Kc5 goes around the c6 pawn. The king cannot stand on c6 while its own pawn occupies it.
a7 leaves only one step to promotion. The pawn is now too far advanced for the king’s illustrated route.
Kb6 gets close but cannot attack a8 in time. A king on b6 attacks a7, so White must promote now.
a8=Q promotes before the king can capture the pawn. The exact queen-versus-four-pawns position is winning for White; the later queen conversion is outside this selected race.
branches.explanation: a8=Q promotes before the king can capture the pawn. The exact queen-versus-four-pawns position is winning for White; the later queen conversion is outside this selected race.

branches.title: Independent reply: move the blocking c-pawn
commentary: Begin after ...bxc6. White has Kg2/a4 against Ke5/c6/d6/f6/h7. Black has four pawns, but c6 and d6 obstruct the king’s direct path toward a8.
a5 starts the same forcing pawn race.
c5 clears c6 for the king, but using a move to clear the square costs Black a tempo. This is an independently selected defense, not an illustrated source line.
a6 advances while Black spends time reorganizing the king’s route.
Kd5 approaches the newly cleared c6 square. Black has not recovered the tempo spent moving the pawn.
a7 keeps the promotion threat immediate.
Kc6 reaches the cleared square, but still does not control a8.
a8=Q promotes safely. Every intermediate outcome remains a White win; clearing the obstruction does not repair the lost tempo.

branches.explanation: a8=Q promotes safely. Every intermediate outcome remains a White win; clearing the obstruction does not repair the lost tempo.

branches.title: Independent error: bring the king first
commentary: Begin after ...bxc6. White has Kg2/a4 against Ke5/c6/d6/f6/h7. Black has four pawns, but c6 and d6 obstruct the king’s direct path toward a8.
Kf2 wastes the essential tempo. Black is now winning with best play; White needed a5 before beginning any king maneuver.
Kd4 begins a winning interception route. This defense and the following moves are independently selected representative replies.
a5 starts the race one move too late.
Kc5 approaches the a-file from below the obstructing pawns.
a6 continues, but Black can now reach b6 before the pawn is ready to promote.
Kb6 attacks a7 and a5. The king has caught up because of White’s initial delay.
a7 steps onto the attacked square. White cannot save this pawn by advancing it now.
Kxa7 removes White’s last pawn. Black’s king and four pawns win against the lone white king; this branch demonstrates the cost of a single wasted tempo.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Kxa7 removes White’s last pawn. Black’s king and four pawns win against the lone white king; this branch demonstrates the cost of a single wasted tempo.

exercises.prompt: Why does having four pawns not let Black stop a single pawn?
exercises.answer: The c6 and d6 pawns occupy squares the black king would like to use. White can exploit that obstruction with an immediate a5; moving the king first loses the tempo advantage.

exercises.prompt: Does moving c6 to c5 solve the problem?
exercises.answer: It clears a king route, but consumes a move. In the independently checked line White keeps pushing and promotes before the black king can control a8.

startContext: This lesson begins in the visually supported seven-piece diagram after ...bxc6 at 117s, when the central pawn barrier is already formed. It verifies the final a-pawn race and two independent comparisons. The earlier larger setup, Kxg2 drawing attempt, f6 sacrifice, a4 breakthrough and d6/c6 sacrifices remain source context and require separate larger-position analysis. A checked promotion race does not verify those earlier choices.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
